items.stem: What should you establish before drafting any business document?

options.rationale: Correct: purpose and audience shape structure, tone and content.
Length is not a goal; clarity is.
Plain language usually communicates better than complex vocabulary.

options.text: The font and colour scheme first
options.rationale: Formatting follows purpose and content, not the reverse.

items.explanation: Correct: clarifying purpose and audience first guides every other writing choice.

items.stem: Which TWO practices make a professional email more effective? (Select TWO)

options.rationale: Correct: a clear subject line tells the reader what to expect and act on.

options.text: Leading with the key message and any request
options.rationale: Correct: putting the key point first respects the reader's time and reduces missed actions.

options.text: Using dense jargon to sound authoritative
options.rationale: Jargon reduces clarity and can confuse readers.

options.text: Copying the whole department on every message
options.rationale: Over-copying creates noise and dilutes accountability.

items.explanation: Correct: a specific subject line and a clear up-front message improve an email.

items.stem: Why should an executive summary be able to stand alone?

options.text: Senior readers may act on it without reading the full document
options.rationale: Correct: an executive summary must convey the conclusion and key support on its own.

options.text: It is only decoration and will not be read
options.rationale: It is often the most-read part, not decoration.
It must state the conclusion up front.

options.text: It must be longer than the report
options.rationale: It is a concise distillation, not longer than the report.

items.explanation: Correct: decision-makers often read only the executive summary, so it must stand alone.
